case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 26th of July, 2012 passed by the High Court Division in civil Revision No. 1201 of 1981.)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 26.07.2012 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1201 of 1981 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that Kushal Mondal, predecessor of the respondents herein as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 275 of 1975 in the Court of the then Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Rajshahi for declaration of title to the suit land. The plaintiff stated, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Askar Mondal, who possessed the same and died leaving behind his brother's son Saber Mondal. Saber Mondal during his lifetime used to possess the suit land and after his death his heir, the original plaintiff Kushal Mondal as his son inherited the property. During S.A. operation, the land in dispute was correctly recorded in the name of the plaintiff and, accordingly, he paid rent to the Government and the Government after accepting him as tenant granted rent receipts in his favour. During R.S. operation, the suit land was erroneously recorded in the name of the defendants. Accordingly, the plaintiffs title to the suit property was doused. Hence, the plaintiff filed the suit.

3. The defendants contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint. Their case, in short, is that the disputed property originally belonged to Askar Mondal. But during his lifetime, he surrendered the same in favour of ex-landlord, who settled the same to one Chhoto Babu Mondal, who died leaving behind defendant Nos.1 and 4 as daughters and one Saira Bewa as wife. Saira Bewa gifted her share in favour of her grandsons, defendant Nos.2 and 3 and one Rahim Uddin Mondal, Rahim Uddin Mondal died leaving behind defendant No.5 as father and defendant No4 as mother. Accordingly, defendant Nos.1-5 had been possessing the suit land after acquiring the same and paid rent to the Government. The R.S. record of the sit property has correctly been published in the names of defendant and possession in the suit land and as such, the suit was liable to be dismissed.

4. On conclusion of hearing the learned Munsif, Rajshahi decreed the suit by his judgment and order dated 19.11.1979. Being aggrieved, the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 123 of 1979 in the Court of District Judge, Rajshahi. On transfer, the appeal was heard by the then Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Rajshahi, who after hearing the parties by judgment and decree dated 19.09.1980 allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. Being aggrieved, the plaintiffs preferred Civil Revision No. 1201 of 1981 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was made absolute. Against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division, defendant Nos. 2-3 filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2355 of 2012 and leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners:

"I. That the trial Court while deciding issue No. 2 found that Saber Mondal is the brother's son of Askar Mondol, who is alleged to have gifted the suit property to his nephew Saber Mondal by 'wasiyatnama' dated 15th Ashar, 1330 B.S. and thus the trial Court made a wrong approach of the whole case and arrived at a wrong decision but the High Court Division without applying its judicial mind to the material aspects of the case made a wrong judgment and as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

II. That the plaintiffs case was that Askar Mondal gifted to his nephew Saber Mondal by 'wasiyatnama' dated 15th Ashar, 1330 B.S. but the appellate Court found that the plaintiff being son of Saber Mondal did not produce the basic document of his title, so the plaintiff hopelessly failed to prove his title in the suit land, but the High Court Division without setting aside that positive finding of the Court of appeal below was wrong to hold that the plaintiff was quite able to prove his title in the land and as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

III. That the defendants' claim was that their names were recorded in S.A. khatian and in support of their claim they called for the record from the local settlement office and it was evidently proved that the volume stood in the names of defendant Nos. 1-4 but the High Court Division without looking into this aspect made the Rule absolute and as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

IV. That R.S. operation is done under section 144(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and it has got presumptive and evidentiary value of correctness but the High Court Division wrongly held that it has got no presumptive value and as such, arrived at a wrong decision and consequently, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside; and

V. That all the D.Ws. corroborated the defendants' claim of possession for 50 years of the suit land but the High Court Division without setting aside this finding of the appellate Court arrived at a wrong decision and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside."

5. Mr. M. Quamrul Hoque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He also submitted that the trial Court in decreeing the suit did not at all discuss the evidence of the DWs of the documents furnished by the defendants. He further submitted that it is an established principle that the weakness in the defence case is not a ground for granting decree in favour of the plaintiff. In support of hus contention he referred to the decision in the case of Md. Naimuddin Sarder & Naimuddin Sarder Vs. Md. Abdul Kalam Biswas @ Md. Abul Kalam Basiruddin & Abul Kalam Azad & anr. Reported in 39 DLR(AD)239, where it was held that, "In the instant case the learned Subordinate Judge proceeded to consider the respective cases of the plaintiff and defendant upon reiterating the age-old axiom that the plaintiff must succeed on his own case and weakness of defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff." He also submitted that the plaintiff did not substantiate his two claims namely, the title of the property through purchase deed and gift in favour of Saber Mondal (father of the plaintiff) by an unregistered deed of gift.

6. Mr. Md. Ali Reza, learned Advocate appearing for respondent Nos.1(a)(i)- 1(a)(vii) and 1(b)-1(e) made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He also submitted that Askar Mondal died leaving Saber Mondal as brother's son who inherited the property left behind by Askar Mondal and subsequently Saber Mondal died leaving son Kushal Mondal and the High Court Division rightly found that Saber Mondal possessed the suit land for more than 12(twelve) years and the S.A. record was duly prepared in the name of the son of Suber Mondal and he paid rents to the Government and, accordingly, the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute. He further submitted that all the P.Ws. categorically proved that the plaintiff is owning and possessing the suit land and the S.A. khatian was rightly prepared in the name of the plaintiff and the defendants miserably failed to prove the basis of the recording of the R.S. khatian in respect of the suit land in their names and accordingly the High Court Division disbelieved the case of the defendants and rightly made the Rule absolute which calls for no interference by this Division. He submitted that the defendants have miserably failed to prove that the original owner of the suit land namely Askar Mondal surrendered the suit land in favour of the ex-landlord and the defendants failed to adduce any documentary evidence and also failed to examine any pertinent witness to prove this issue and as such, the High Court Division has rightly made the Rule absolute which calls for no interference by this Division. He submitted that the defendants have failed to prove by adducing any documentary evidence that after surrender of the suit land by Askar Mondal, when the ex-landlord took the same in his khas possession and also when he settled the same to Chhoto Babu Mondal (the predecessor-in-interest of defendant No.1-5), and the trial Court and the High Court Division rightly found that that the defendants miserably failed to prove their case and, therefore, the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute which calls for no interference by this Division. He submitted that P.V1s.4 and 5 are independent witnesses who clearly stated in the deposition that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land and they have land near the suit land and that the High Court Division rightly believed the evidentiary value of the deposition of these two independent witnesses and observed that the witnesses of the defendants contradicted themselves in their depositions in respect of possession of the suit land their testimony is not cogent and credible and, therefore the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute which calls for no interference by this Division. He also submitted that the Court of appeal below, as the final Court of fact, did not discuss and consider a single witness examined by the contesting parties while reversing the judgment of the trial Court as is required by Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He lastly submitted that the High Court Division as well as the trial Court rightly came to a finding that the plaintiff proved his title and possession in the suit land and the defendants have miserably failed to prove their title and possession in the suit land and hence the impugned judgment calls for no interference by this Division.

7. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

<u>8. At the outset we are constrained to hold that the finding of the High Court Division to the effect that, "It is the established principle of civil law that the R.S. records of rights have got no presumptive value of its correctness "such observation is clearly contrary to section 114 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, of which the relevant provisions are reproduced here:-</u>

<u>144. Revision of record-of-rights -(1) The Government may in any case if it thinks fit make an order directing that a record-of-rights in respect of any district, part of a district or local area be prepared or revised by a Revenue-officer, in accordance with such rule as may be made by the Government in this behalf.</u>

<u>(3) A notification in the official Gazette of an order under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence that the order has been duly made.</u>

<u>(4) When an order is made under sub-section (1), the Revenue-officer shall record in the record-of-rights to be pre-pared or revised in pursuance of such order such particulars as may be pre-scribed.</u>

<u>(5)When a record-of-rights has been prepared or revised so as to contain or include therein the particulars referred to in sub-section (4), and rents assessed or re-assessed under sub-section (4a), the Revenue-officer shall publish a draft of the record-of-rights so pre-pared or revised in the prescribed manner and for the prescribed period and shall receive and consider any objections which may be made to any entry therein or to any omissions therefrom during the period of such publication.</u>

<u>(6) Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Revenue-officer on any objection made under sub-section (5) may prefer an appeal to the prescribed Revenue Authority not below the rank of an Assistant Settlement Officer in such manner and within such period as may be prescribed.</u>

<u>(7) When all such objections and appeals have been considered and dis-posed of according to such rules as the Government may make in this behalf, the Revenue-officer shall finally frame the record and shall cause such record to be finally published in the pre-scribed manner and the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly prepared or revised under this section.</u>

<u>(8) When a record-of-rights has been finally published under sub-section(7), the Revenue-officer shall, within such time as the Director of Land Records and Surveys may fix in this behalf, make a certificate stating the fact of such final publication and the date thereof and shall date and subscribe the same with his name and official title. 144A. Presumption as to correctness of record of rights-Every entry in a record-of-rights prepared or revised under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect."</u>

9. The learned Judge appears to have over-looked the provision of section 114 illustration (e) of the Evidence Act which provides as follows:-

"114 Court may presume existence of certain facts-The Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business, in their relation to the facts of the particular case.

Illustrations

10. The Court may presume-

(e)that judicial and official acts have been regularly performed;"

11. Hence, there can be no doubt that the record of rights in the names of the defendants creates a rebuttable presumption in their favour.

12. The plaintiff claims title in the suit land by way of inheritance from Saber Mondal who was the nephew of the original owner, namely Askar Mondal. The S.A. record was in the name of the plaintiff, but the R.S. record for the suit land was wrongly in the name of the defendants. On the other hand the defendants claim that the original owner Askar Mondal surrendered the suit land in favour of the superior landlord who settled the land in favour of Chhoto Babu Mondal more than 50 years previously and the land is now in the possession of the successors of said Chhoto Babu Mondal. They also claimed that the documents produced by the plaintiff were forged.

<u>13. It is a cardinal principle of law that the plaintiff must prove his case in order to get a decree in his favour. Time and again this Court has held that the weakness of the defendants case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff (see of Md. Naimuddin Sarder @ Naimuddin Sarder Vs. Md. Abdul Kalam Biswas @ Md. Abul Kalam Basiruddin @ Abul Kalam Azad & anr reported in 39 DLR(AD)237 and also Khondoker Mobarak Ali -vs- Jahanara Begun and others reported in 1 ADC 401.)</u>

14. The moot question in the instant case is whether the plaintiff was able to prove that title in the suit land passed to him through his father Saber Mondal who was the brother of the original owner Askar Mondal. The trial Court decreed the suit upon observing that, "It has not been challenged by the defendants that the plaintiff is not the brother's son of Askar Mondal." The trial Court also relied on the fact that the S.A. record was in the name of the plaintiff, which was also supported by rent receipts showing that the government realised rent for the suit land from the plaintiff up to 1967 (1374 B.S.) admitting the plaintiff as tenant. The trial Court also observed that the defendants, did not adduce any evidence to prove that the ex-landlord got the suit land in his khas possession after surrender by Askar Mondal or that Chhoto Babu Mondal got settlement.

<u>15. However, we find from the cross-examination of the plaintiff (P.W.1) that he was in fact challenged with regard to his claim that his father was the brother of Askar Mondal. Hence, the observation of the trial Court clearly shows misreading of the evidence. Moreover, the trial Court appears to have overlooked the plaintiffs contradictory claim that "Askar Mondal during his lifetime also gifted the S.L. to my father by executing the unregistered deed". The trial Court also disbelieved the defendants' case of surrender and pattan because no supporting evidence was adduced. The trial Court thus fell into error in shifting the burden of proof on to the defendants. We further note that the trial Court did not discuss the evidence of the DWs or the documents produced by the defendants.</u>

16. The appellate Court, on the other hand identified three distinct claims made by the plaintiff in respect of his ownership of the suit land, viz-by way of Kabala dated 02.11.1937; deed of gift; and by way of inheritance. It was observed by the appellate Court that the plaintiff did not produce either the kabala or the deed of gift in order to prove the basis of his claim, nor was any explanation given in the plaint or in the amendment petition for non-production of his basic documents.

17. Although the plaintiff claimed title to the land with support from Ext-1 the S.A. Khatian, he did not challenge the genuineness of the original volume of the S.A. record, which was, produced before the appellate Court at the instance of the defendants. The appellate Court found on penisal of the volume in question that the suit property was duly recorded in the name of defendant Nos. 1-4 in the name of one Saira Bewa, wife of Chhoto Babu Mondal. In allowing the appeal by the defendants, the appellate Court took into consideration the rent receipts produced by the defendants showing payment of rent to the government.

18. In view of the above facts and circumstances, it is abundantly clear that the judgment and decree of the trial court was patently erroneous and based upon misreading of evidence. The appellate Court properly reversed the judgment of the trial Court. Evidently the claim of the plaintiff was falsified by the production of the S.A. record of rights, which falsified the claim of the plaintiff and, on the other hand, proved that the S.A. records were in the names of the defendants.

19. As noted earlier, the judgment of the High Court Division is palpably erroneous, being contrary to settled principle of law and wrong interpretation of statute.

20. In view of the above discussions, we find merit in the appeal, which is accordingly allowed, without however, any order as to costs.

21. The judgment and order of the High Court Division is hereby set aside.

End.
